stories.title: Lal Bihari Mritak
stories.description: Amit tells the tragicomic story of Lal Bihari, a man from UP who was declared dead by his cousins to steal his land. He spent 18 years trying to prove he was alive, even kidnapping a cousin and throwing stones at police to get arrested (and thus prove his existence).

stories.title: Al Capone and Laundromats
stories.description: Ajay explains that the term 'money laundering' originated from Al Capone, who bought laundromats (cash businesses) to mix his illegal bootlegging profits with legitimate cash income.

stories.title: Harsh Vardhan's KYC Nightmare
stories.description: Amit shares that even Harsh Vardhan, a senior banking figure and consultant, struggled to navigate the KYC maze, highlighting that if the elite can't manage it, the poor have no chance.

stories.title: Russian Officials and US Treasury
stories.description: Ajay recounts an anecdote where Russian officials told an Indian official that the US Treasury taught them how to build a financial surveillance system to oppress their own people.

stories.title: Exploding Breast Implants
stories.description: Amit mentions a news story about terrorists planning to use breast implants as bombs to illustrate the absurdity of 'security theater'—we can't ask people to put their implants in a tray.

core_ideas.description: Just as we have personal privacy, we should have financial privacy. A liberal democracy cannot exist if the state has mass surveillance over every financial transaction.
In a free society, privacy should be the default. Surveillance should only be permitted with a judicial warrant, for a specific suspect, and for a finite time.
Systems that monitor everyone (like current AML/CFT regimes) are fundamentally illiberal. The state should not treat every citizen as a potential criminal.
Ajay traces the history of financial surveillance from the Nazis (1933) to the US Bank Secrecy Act (1970) and the post-9/11 Patriot Act, showing how 'emergency' measures became permanent oppression.
Much of what passes for security (airport checks, KYC) is 'theater' designed to make the state look like it's doing something, without actually stopping determined terrorists.
Adding technology (like Aadhaar) to a broken institution (the Indian state) does not fix the problem. It just makes the oppression more efficient or adds another layer of complexity.
Complex KYC/AML rules disproportionately hurt the poor and small businesses, who cannot afford the compliance costs, driving them out of the formal financial system.
